"This is why we all love the Olympic Games. Because through you, we see the very best of ourselves. You remind us that we can be brave. That we can be kind. And that we can get back up, no matter how hard we fall.

And to everyone watching, here in Italy and around the world – thank you for joining this moment. Thank you for believing in the magic of the Olympic Games.

When we see an athlete stumble and find the strength to rise, we are reminded that we can do the same.

When we see rivals embrace at the end of a finish line, we are reminded that we can choose respect.

When we see grace, courage and friendship – we remember the kind of people we all want to be.

The spirit of the Olympic Games is about so much more than sport. It is about us – and what makes us human.

In Africa, where I’m from, we have a word: ubuntu. It means: I am because we are. That we can only rise by lifting others. That our strength comes from caring for each other.

No matter where you come from, we all know this spirit – it lives and breathes in every community.
I see this spirit most clearly at the Olympic Games. Here, athletes from every corner of our world compete fiercely – but also respect, support and inspire one another. They remind us that we are all connected, that our strength comes from how we treat each other, and that the best of humanity is found in courage, compassion and kindness.

So let these Games be a celebration of what unites us – of everything that makes us human.

This is the magic of the Olympic Games: inspiring us all to be the best that we can be – together."
She's Zimbabwean, the first woman and first African IOC president. Paste the lines you want from the IOC's own transcript; keep any single quote short.

## How to invest, without a savior complex

<!-- ~75 sec  

1. **Fund operations, not just ribbon-cuttings.**
2. **Go where the players already are.**
3. **Lower the cost of entry:** fees, travel, free play.
4. **Let local leaders set the agenda.** Fund for years, not photo ops.
5. **Count everyone.** Publish who plays, who quits, and why.

::: {.notes}
Anchors: (1) Cape Town's maintenance gap; (2) Athlone vs. Green Point; (3) Project Play
on travel and fees; (4) Coventry has said African infrastructure, including for the
All Africa Games, needs to improve before credible Olympic bids; (5) this is your
statistician's contribution: the denominators.
Phrase it as "back" and "fund," not "bring" or "save."
:::

# Noise {background-color="#1b5635"}

## A striker is 9-for-10 on penalties

<!-- ~45 sec  

**It's a shootout Saturday. Is he your designated taker?**

. . .

Raw math says 90%. Your gut says *"...it's ten kicks."*

. . .

Ten kicks is a grainy photo. You can't tell a face from a smudge.

. . .

What helps is what you already know about what you're looking at:
[penalties go in about three in four times]{.placeholder}. That's a **prior**.

::: {.notes}
Setup only. The tension: the raw number is the only thing on screen, but you carry
two pieces of information, the league rate and his ten kicks. Bayesian statistics
is the rule for combining them.
:::

## Prior + evidence = posterior

<!-- ~75 sec  

$$
\theta \sim \text{Beta}(31,\,9) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\theta \mid \text{9 makes, 1 miss} \sim \text{Beta}(40,\,10)
$$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 9
a0 <- 31; b0 <- 9            # illustrative prior: ~77% average, worth ~40 kicks
made <- 9; n <- 10
a1 <- a0 + made; b1 <- b0 + (n - made)
x     <- seq(0.4, 1, length.out = 500)
prior <- dbeta(x, a0, b0)
post  <- dbeta(x, a1, b1)
p_better <- 1 - pbeta(a0 / (a0 + b0), a1, b1)
plot(x, post, type = "l", lwd = 4, col = "#C68346",
     xlab = "True penalty conversion rate", ylab = "", yaxt = "n", bty = "n",
     ylim = c(0, max(prior, post) * 1.1), cex.lab = 1.3, cex.axis = 1.2)
lines(x, prior, lwd = 4, col = "#1b5635", lty = 2)
abline(v = 0.90, lty = 3, lwd = 2)
text(0.90, max(prior, post) * 0.9, "Raw: 90%", pos = 2, cex = 1.2)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 1.2, lwd = 4,
       col = c("#1b5635", "#C68346"), lty = c(2, 1),
       legend = c("Prior (league-level belief)",
                  paste0("Posterior (mean ~", round(100 * a1 / (a1 + b1)), "%)")))
mtext(paste0("P(better than average) = ", round(p_better, 2)),
      side = 3, line = 0, cex = 1.1)
```

. . .

The update is addition: 31 + 9 makes, 9 + 1 miss. And the answer is a **distribution**,
so you can ask: *how likely is he actually better than average?*

::: {.notes}
Prior Beta(31, 9), mean 77.5%, worth about 40 kicks. Posterior Beta(40, 10), mean
80%. A decision-maker doesn't need "80%." They need "two in three odds he's better
than average, and here's how much to trust that." A point estimate can't give you that.
:::

## The prior is an assumption, said out loud

<!-- ~60 sec  

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 9
priors <- list(`Weak prior`     = c(3.1, 0.9),
               `Moderate prior` = c(31, 9),
               `Strong prior`   = c(77.5, 22.5))
cols <- c("#C68346", "#1b5635", "#6a6a6a")
ltys <- c(1, 2, 3)
obs  <- list(c(9, 10), c(90, 100))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 1, 3, 1))
for (d in obs) {
  x  <- seq(0.5, 1, length.out = 500)
  ys <- lapply(priors, function(p) dbeta(x, p[1] + d[1], p[2] + d[2] - d[1]))
  plot(x, ys[[1]], type = "l", lwd = 3, col = cols[1], lty = ltys[1],
       xlab = "True conversion rate", ylab = "", yaxt = "n", bty = "n",
       ylim = c(0, max(unlist(ys)) * 1.1), cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1,
       main = paste0(d[1], " of ", d[2], " kicks"), cex.main = 1.3)
  for (i in 2:3) lines(x, ys[[i]], lwd = 3, col = cols[i], lty = ltys[i])
  if (d[2] == 10) legend("topleft", bty = "n", cex = 1.0, lwd = 3,
                         col = cols, lty = ltys, legend = names(priors))
}
```

. . .

With ten kicks, your assumption matters. With a hundred, the data takes over.
More exposures sharpen the picture.

. . .

Every model has a prior. A model that doesn't show you one is still using it.

::: {.notes}
Weak prior is worth about 4 kicks, moderate about 40, strong about 100. The usual
objection to Bayes is "isn't the prior just your opinion?" Answer: yes, and it is
stated, adjustable, and overwhelmed by evidence. This sets up the NBA project:
thousands of players is the right-hand panel.
:::

## My own project: does pedigree predict a longer NBA career?

<!-- ~75 sec  

*With Jonas Schiel.* "Blue blood" programs: Duke, North Carolina, UCLA, Indiana,
Kentucky, Kansas.

. . .

Career length is a count, right-skewed. Model: **Poisson likelihood, Gamma prior.**
Prior expectation: about 5 years for blue-blood alumni, about 3.5 for everyone else.

. . .

Same logic as the penalties. Different conjugate pair, much more data.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-width: 9
lo  <- c(5.09, 4.27); hi <- c(5.51, 4.40)
par(mar = c(4.5, 10, 1, 1))
plot(NULL, xlim = c(3.8, 6), ylim = c(0.5, 2.5), yaxt = "n", bty = "n",
     xlab = "Mean career length (years), 95% credible interval", ylab = "",
     cex.lab = 1.3, cex.axis = 1.2)
segments(lo, c(2, 1), hi, c(2, 1), lwd = 10, col = c("#C68346", "#1b5635"), lend = 1)
axis(2, at = c(2, 1), labels = c("Blue-blood alumni", "Everyone else"),
     las = 1, tick = FALSE, cex.axis = 1.2)
```

::: {.notes}
Numbers from your write-up: 95% CI for mean career length (5.09, 5.51) vs (4.27,
4.40); difference (0.74, 1.19). Likely questions:
(1) "Didn't you pick different priors for each group?" Yes (5 vs 3.5 years). With
this much data the intervals are driven by the data, but the cleanest answer is a
sensitivity check: refit with the SAME prior for both groups and report that the
conclusion holds. Do this before you present if you can; it turns a vulnerability
into the strongest slide.
(2) "Is Poisson right?" Poisson forces variance = mean and allows zero years; real
careers are overdispersed and at least one year. Say you treated it as a known
simplification (your write-up already does) and that a negative binomial or
zero-truncated model would be the next step.
:::

## What the model can and can't say

<!-- ~60 sec  

| Career longer than | Blue-blood | Everyone else |
|:------------------:|:----------:|:-------------:|
| 5 years            | **42.8%**  | 27.1%         |
| 10 years           | 1.8%       | 0.76%         |

. . .

There's a real gap: the 95% credible interval for the difference is 0.74 to 1.19 years.

. . .

What I can't say: that the **school** causes it. Top prospects pick top programs.
And the model treats each season as independent, which careers aren't.

. . .

::: {.big-statement}
Knowing what your model can't say is part of the model.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the "Noise" test applied to your own work: a real, quantified difference,
reported with its limits. Next step you named in the write-up: control for draft
position, era, and position; or update the blue-blood definition (UCLA). If asked
"so does it matter?": it predicts, it doesn't prove cause.
:::

# Backup # 2{background-color="#6a6a6a"}

## What predicts an NHL player's plus-minus?

<!-- Backup: Q&A / interviews  

*With Claire Peterson and Anzlei Larsen.* Multiple linear regression, 1,000-iteration
cross-validation, NHL seasons 2000-01 to 2024-25.

. . .

**Adjusted R² = 0.123.** Cross-validated RMSE 0.157, effectively unbiased.

. . .

We reported 12% as the finding, not the failure. Hockey is noisy, and the variables
that probably matter (team quality, age, coaching system) weren't in the data.

::: {.notes}
Shooting percentage had the strongest positive association, then position
(defensemen and centers), assists, and shots per game. Interactive explorer:
nhl-explorer.streamlit.app. Interview use: "I know what my model can't do, and I say so."
:::

## Do it for the whole squad

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 9
set.seed(7)
N     <- 150
theta <- rbeta(N, 31, 9)                  # each player's true rate (simulated)
n     <- sample(3:30, N, replace = TRUE)  # kicks taken: some players have very few
made  <- rbinom(N, n, theta)
raw   <- made / n
shr   <- (31 + made) / (40 + n)
rmse  <- function(e) sqrt(mean((e - theta)^2))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1))
plot(theta, raw, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("#C68346", 0.6), cex = 1.1,
     xlim = c(0.5, 1), ylim = c(0.2, 1),
     xlab = "True rate", ylab = "Estimated rate", cex.lab = 1.2,
     main = paste0("Raw rate (error ", round(rmse(raw), 3), ")"), cex.main = 1.2)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
plot(theta, shr, pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("#1b5635", 0.6), cex = 1.1,
     xlim = c(0.5, 1), ylim = c(0.2, 1),
     xlab = "True rate", ylab = "", cex.lab = 1.2,
     main = paste0("With a prior (error ", round(rmse(shr), 3), ")"), cex.main = 1.2)
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
```

Players with 3 kicks and players with 30 shouldn't be trusted equally. Shrink each
estimate in proportion to how little you know.

::: {.notes}
Simulated; we know the true rates so we can score the estimates. Partial pooling in
its simplest form. In practice the prior's parameters are estimated from the whole
population (empirical Bayes) or modeled hierarchically.
:::

## The same team, 10,000 seasons

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-width: 9
set.seed(42)
p   <- c(win = 0.30, draw = 0.27, loss = 0.43)   # illustrative mid-table team
pts <- replicate(10000, { r <- rmultinom(1, 38, p); 3 * r[1] + r[2] })
ci  <- quantile(pts, c(0.05, 0.95))
hist(pts, breaks = seq(min(pts) - 0.5, max(pts) + 0.5, 1),
     col = "#C68346", border = "white", main = "",
     xlab = "Season points (38 games)", ylab = "", yaxt = "n",
     cex.lab = 1.3, cex.axis = 1.2)
abline(v = 38 * (3 * p["win"] + p["draw"]), lwd = 3, lty = 2, col = "#1b5635")
abline(v = ci, lwd = 2, lty = 3)
legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 1.2,
       legend = paste0("90% of seasons: ", ci[1], " to ", ci[2], " points"))
```

Identical team. Identical strength. The only thing that changed was luck.

::: {.notes}
Backup for "what does unlucky mean." Illustrative win/draw/loss probabilities for a
middling team; say so.
::: -->

## But who gets an invitation?

The cost of being a fan can be high.

The cost of playing can be even higher.

- Ticket prices can put major events out of reach.
- Youth sports costs have risen.
- Travel and equipment can make participation difficult for families.

Girls' participation in high school sports has grown dramatically over time.

That matters—but participation alone does not prove equal access, resources, or outcomes.

## Hope requires investment

- Fund the people and programs already doing the work.
- Reduce the cost of getting started.
- Follow local leadership.
- Count who is still missing.

# OPTION 2 — When the Numbers Miss the Point
## There are lies, damned lies, and statistics

A familiar line often attributed to Mark Twain.

But the important question isn't whether statistics lie.

**It's whether we are asking them the right question.**

::: {.notes}
Target: about 10 minutes. Be careful with the attribution: the saying is commonly attributed to Mark Twain, but the origin is disputed. You can say “a familiar saying” instead.
:::

## A statistic can reveal—and hide

::: {.big-statement}
A statistic can show you something important while hiding the context that changes its meaning.
:::

A model can calculate an answer correctly and still answer the wrong question.

::: {.notes}
This is a paraphrase, not a direct quotation. The point is not that statistics are useless, but that interpreting them requires context and judgment.
:::

## The model I thought I needed

In the BYU Sports Analytics Association, I worked on an NHL modeling competition.

The goal: predict the plus-minus leaders for hockey at the Winter Olympics.

My first instinct could have been to rely on historical Olympic data.

But there was a problem.

::: {.notes}
Briefly explain plus-minus for the audience: a player receives a plus or minus based on goals scored while they are on the ice at even strength, with some special-team situations excluded. Keep the exact definition consistent with the competition's metric.
:::

## The context changed

The 2026 Winter Olympics marked the return of NHL players to Olympic men's hockey for the first time since **2014**.

The 2025 Four Nations Face-Off offered recent best-on-best international hockey involving NHL players.

Past Olympic tournaments did not necessarily represent the same player pool or competition conditions.

::: {.notes}
Check the competition dates and your original analysis. The last Olympics with NHL players was 2014, not 2010. Be precise about which Four Nations statistics you used and why they were relevant to the prediction task.
:::

## A better comparison

Instead of treating past Olympic results as automatically relevant, I used the Four Nations tournament as evidence for predicting the Olympic leaders.

**The key decision was not just how to model the data. It was deciding which data were relevant.**

::: {.notes}
Fill in the specifics before presenting:
- Which Four Nations statistics did you use?
- Did you combine them with regular-season NHL statistics?
- How did you turn those data into a predicted ranking?
- What was the competition's scoring rule, and how did your entry perform?

Do not claim the change caused the win unless you can explain the scoring and comparison clearly.
:::

## Three questions before trusting a model

**1. Relevance:** Does the data resemble the situation I'm predicting?

**2. Change:** What is different this time?

**3. Decision:** Does the model answer the question the audience actually needs answered?

::: {.notes}
Return to the Olympics example for each question. The player pool and tournament context affected relevance; the Olympic format and timing affected what could reasonably be compared; the final goal was to predict leaders, not explain every aspect of hockey.
:::

## A model is not a substitute for judgment

Models help us organize evidence, quantify uncertainty, and make predictions.

But the analyst still has to decide:

- What belongs in the data?
- Which assumptions are reasonable?
- What has changed since the historical examples?
- What would make the prediction useful?

::: {.notes}
Avoid saying critical thinking is always better than modeling. In your story, critical thinking helped you select a more appropriate source of evidence. That is the stronger claim.
:::

## The point isn't to reject statistics

It is to use them with care.

The number is not the whole story. The model is not the whole problem.

::: {.big-statement}
Ask the right question.

Choose relevant evidence.

Then decide how much to trust the answer.
:::

::: {.notes}
End with the NHL story: the useful insight was noticing the context that made one source of evidence more relevant than another. Aim for a 30–40-second close.
:::
